memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: 'They must make full restitution for the wrong they have done, add a fifth of the value to it and give it all to the person they have wronged. But if that person has no close relative to whom restitution can be made for the wrong, the restitution belongs to the Lord and must be given to the priest, along with the ram with which atonement is made for the wrongdoer.' - Num 5:7b-8 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Confession is the first step, but God asks for more: restitution. The wrongdoer had to repay what was taken, and add a fifth on top. True repentance is not only words of sorrow; where possible, it seeks to make things right.

This is a searching truth. It is easy to say "sorry" and move on, leaving the damage unrepaired. But biblical repentance rolls up its sleeves. If we have taken something, we return it. If we have caused harm, we do what we can to mend it. Sorrow that costs us nothing is often shallow sorrow.

We see this beautifully in the New Testament when Zacchaeus met Jesus. His changed heart showed itself at once in action: he gave back what he had wrongly taken, and more (Luke 19:8). Grace had transformed him, and restitution flowed out.

We must be careful, though. Restitution does not earn God's forgiveness — that comes through Christ alone. Notice that even in this passage, atonement was made through a ram. The making-right toward people flowed alongside the atonement that put things right with God.

Because Christ has paid our debt to God, we are freed to make our debts right with others. Is there something you need to return, repair, or repay today? Grace received becomes grace lived out.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Is there a wrong you need to actively make right?
- Does your repentance show itself in action, not just words?
- How does Christ's atonement free you to make things right with others?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, thank You that Christ has made me right with You. Now give me the humility and courage to make right the wrongs I have done to others. Amen.
